lessons.title: Water, land and climate as aquaculture resources
lessons.html:
Aquaculture depends on the environment

Fish farms draw on water, land, climate and biodiversity, and they return water and nutrients to the environment. A farm manager must understand both what the environment provides and how the farm affects it.

Water sources

SourceStrengthsRisks
BoreholeStable temperature, usually free of wild fish and pathogensLow oxygen, high carbon dioxide or iron, limited yield, pumping cost
River or streamLarge volumes, gravity flow possibleSilt, pollution, wild fish diseases, flow drops in drought
Farm damStorage through dry seasonTemperature swings, algal blooms, evaporation
MunicipalReliable qualityChlorine is toxic to fish, cost

South Africa is a water-scarce country, and water allocation is controlled under the National Water Act 36 of 1998. A farm must hold the correct water use authorisation for taking water, storing it and discharging used water.

Climate

Climate determines which species can be farmed economically. Warm-water species such as tilapia and catfish suit the warmer lowveld and coastal areas or heated systems; trout suit cool, high-altitude areas such as parts of Mpumalanga and the Western Cape mountains. Consider frost, heat waves, rainfall pattern, evaporation and the likelihood of drought and floods.

Land and soils

Earth ponds need soils with enough clay to hold water, a gentle slope for gravity filling and draining, and a site above flood level. Avoid wetlands and river banks, which are environmentally sensitive and often need authorisation to develop. The Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 also governs use of agricultural land and protection of soil and vegetation.

Energy

Pumping and aeration consume much electricity. Site choice (gravity flow), efficient equipment and solar power can lower both cost and the farm's footprint.

lessons.title: Environmental impacts and responsible practice
lessons.html:
How fish farms affect the environment

Responsible aquaculture keeps the farm's impact within what the surrounding environment can absorb. This also protects the farm, which needs clean water itself.

Effluent and nutrients

Uneaten feed and fish waste add nitrogen, phosphorus and solids to discharge water. Downstream this can cause algal blooms and low oxygen. Reduce the load by feeding efficiently, using settling ponds or constructed wetlands before discharge, and reusing nutrient-rich water or sludge for irrigation or crops where suitable, as in aquaponics.

Escapes and alien species

Several farmed species are not native to many South African catchments, including trout and Nile tilapia. Escaped fish can compete with or prey on indigenous fish and spread disease. The National Environmental Management: Biodiversity Act 10 of 2004 regulates alien and invasive species, and permits may be needed to keep or move them. Prevent escapes with secure screens on outlets, sound pond walls, and care during harvesting and transport. Check with the provincial conservation authority which species and permits apply in your area.

Disease transfer

Pathogens can pass between farmed and wild fish in both directions. Biosecurity, careful disposal of dead fish and treated water, and not releasing farm fish protect wild populations.

Chemicals

Use only registered remedies, at label rates, and keep treated water from being discharged straight into rivers where the label or authorities prohibit this. Store chemicals securely to prevent spills.

Predators and wildlife

Herons, cormorants, kingfishers, otters and monitor lizards are attracted to fish farms. Use exclusion methods such as nets and fencing. Many of these animals are protected; do not kill them, and seek advice from the conservation authority on legal control.

Environmental management on the farm

  • Monitor discharge water quality and keep records.
  • Keep buffer zones of natural vegetation along watercourses.
  • Control erosion around ponds and roads.
  • Manage waste: feed bags, oil, dead fish and chemical containers.

The National Environmental Management Act 107 of 1998 sets the general duty of care to avoid or minimise environmental harm.

Key points

  • Each water source has strengths and risks; match it to the system.
  • Hold the correct water use authorisation.
  • Treat effluent and feed efficiently to limit nutrient pollution.
  • Prevent escapes of alien species and check permit requirements.
  • Use exclusion, not killing, for protected predators.

quiz.question: Why is municipal water risky for fish unless treated?

options.text: It contains chlorine, which is toxic to fish

quiz.question: Which water source usually has a stable temperature but may be low in oxygen?
Which law regulates alien and invasive species in South Africa?

options.text: Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997
National Environmental Management: Biodiversity Act 10 of 2004

quiz.question: What is a good way to reduce nutrients in discharge water?

options.text: Feed more to grow fish faster
Discharge straight into the river at night
Use settling ponds or constructed wetlands

quiz.question: Herons are eating fish from the ponds. What is the responsible response?

options.text: Use nets and other exclusion, and get advice on legal control
